projects.title: How Can I Not Forget
projects.logline: In a near-future Los Angeles where traumatic memories can be erased, a grieving woman begins to remember the massacre — and the truth about her mother's death — someone she loves has been trying to make her forget.
diary: The design projects Nora's internal state onto physical space, and keeps pressing the question of what's real. The apartment is high-class and a little too clean; the hospital has no trace of humanity in it — both built on a rigid, structural order, the kind a world keeps when it's hiding something.
The surgery room is the piece I keep returning to: its clear curtain drape is the whole film in one object — something you see through and still can't see the truth behind.

items.alt: How Can I Not Forget — ORION search prop
items.description: ORION is the film’s near-future search engine — the web on Nora’s laptop. When she looks up the massacre and the riot, the results come back filtered: an overview that explains them away, and a notice that results were “excluded pending verification.” It’s how the state quietly erases what happened. The search, results, and articles are all built and clickable.

key.alt: How Can I Not Forget — The Surgery Room

blocks.text: Much of the film keeps a thin film between Nora and reality. Here it became physical: clear plastic curtains around the surgical table. While she and her husband are on opposite sides of it, the illusion holds. Once they're both inside, there's nothing left between them and the truth. But did she really like the truth better?

blocks.text: The shots stay close on the characters, with close-ups and symmetry, so every set either had to stay quiet or push that emphasis. This is the one room that pushes. Shot on the standing hospital set at Heritage Props, who rigged round curtain tracks on the ceiling for us; we hung the curtains to enclose the table.

key.alt: How Can I Not Forget — The Apartment

blocks.text: The film is less a timeline than an emotional state: doubt, the feeling that something isn't quite right. The couple's apartment had to feel logically homey but emotionally distant, calming to the point of feeling unreal, as if Nora were living inside an illustration.

key.alt: How Can I Not Forget — Nora

blocks.text: Nora's color is olive: grey enough to read as dull, the everyday adulthood that is its own kind of illusion. Its light tint of beige and green is the most natural thing in her world, set against the film's artificial blues. Nature stands for truth, and the only existence she can confirm is her own.

imgs.alt: Costume sketches for Nora
Mourning-wear references

blocks.caption: Costume sketches for Nora; mourning-wear references.

blocks.text: Layers and outerwear build up as she grows defensive; in a tank top or the patient gown she's raw and helpless. Her husband dresses for what he wants to uphold: professionalism, his craft, the strict system he belongs to. Between the two of them: clean against patterned, neutral against vibrant, geometric against floral: the duality of man and nature.

blocks.text: is an AI-enhanced search engine that belongs to Nora's world. When she looks up the massacre, the results come back filtered: an overview that explains it away, and a notice that results were "excluded pending verification." The film's memory-erasing technology has a parallel in how AI is folding into everyday life now, and ORION is where the two meet. I built it as a working site with Claude Code; the search, the results and the articles are all clickable.

projects.title: Sonata
projects.logline: Two Korean-American sisters — one at the piano, one at the violin — circle a childhood duet they could never play together, until their mother's illness finally brings them to the same song.
diary: Sonata takes place in one Korean-American family home, and the design leans all the way into its clutter — the lived-in mess of a house three people have filled over years. I dressed it full: stacked mail and sheet music, medicine and tea sets, framed certificates and small violin trophies on every ledge, laundry drying on a rack in the middle of the living room. The mess isn't background; it holds the tangle between a mother and her two daughters, and the piano they all circle sits at the center of it.

projects.title: Soup 湯
projects.logline: A grieving woman running her family's three-generation Chinese restaurant is offered Meng Po's soup — one sip to forget everything and be reborn — until a young apprentice gives her a reason to hold on instead.
diary: The restaurant in the script is a small, worn room — the kind a family keeps for three generations. What we found was the opposite: too big, too open, nothing that felt lived in. So we made it smaller. We built a wall.

The work split cleanly. I designed the structure — the beams and supports that had to stand on their own on set. Ariel, our production designer, designed the look and led the texturing: layer over layer until fresh drywall read as years, a plexiglass window cut in, graphics and props dressed across it until the seam was gone. By the end, the wall had always been there.

credits.name: Adrianne Meave, Eri Wong, Varshini Satoor, Ying (Diana) Zhang, Yining (Coco) Zhong, Yunlei Liu

projects.title: Antidote
projects.logline: A feverish boy and a world-weary stranger share a hospital ward, where a tin of mints — passed off as painkillers — becomes a quiet mercy that keeps a family from breaking apart.
diary: Antidote unfolds in a single hospital ward — a sick boy and a worn-out stranger sharing a room while the boy's parents carry in the weight of the world outside. I designed the costumes to hold that split. The boy and the old man wear grounded, human color — warm reds and soft, desaturated earth tones, the palette of skin and of being cared for.

The parents were the variable. Their clothes shift with their state of mind across the film — cooling toward something harder and more capitalistic when the money takes hold of them, then warming and lightening in the moments they stop being a provider and a caretaker and become, again, just a mother and a father.

The most deliberate piece was the jacket. People shed a jacket or pull one on as they enter or leave a room, but the gesture is also armor — putting it on raises a guard against the outside, taking it off lets it fall. And with nowhere to source a child's hospital gown, I made one: cutting an adult gown apart and sewing it back down to a boy's size.

credits.name: Arwen Wang, Sifan Liu, Yining Dai

projects.title: On the River Bank
projects.logline: A dance-driven music video that follows Mia through a mist-soaked forest as she chases an illusory success — past a breakfast of empty dishes and scattered poppies, a grove of mirrors hung from the trees, and a path of unreachable lamps — until she reaches the riverbank, and the selves she gathered along the way.
diary: The director set four symbols — flower, mirror, river, chain — and the whole world was built from dressed, found objects in an LA creek bed: a full breakfast table laid with empty china and scattered poppies, salvaged mirrors and lampshades staked through the trees, an ankle shackle, and a gradient-brown gown that bleeds toward red as Mia comes apart.

credits.name: Charlotte Hou, Eri Wong, Yilong Yang

projects.title: Before Sunrise
projects.logline: On what may be the last night before the swelling sun swallows the Earth, Emily, an eighteen-year-old call girl, lets in George, the neighbor who talks her into phoning everyone they know to save the world.

blocks.text: Before Sunrise is a film about internal space: one room as a picture of Emily's inner state. The clutter is the resentment she carries toward everything in her life that fell short, piling up with nowhere to go. It's also what she traps herself in, and protects herself with.

imgs.alt: Atmosphere painting of the room
The room on screen

blocks.caption: Atmosphere painting of the room; the room on screen.

blocks.text: I leaned a little into the stereotypes of sex work: fashion, glamour, womanhood. Not to define her with a label, but to show the deceptive mask that shields her deeper self, a human soul. Clothing hangs everywhere, dressing her and confining her at the same time.

imgs.alt: Clothing strung across the room on lines and racks
Clothing strung across the room on lines and racks

blocks.caption: Clothing strung across the room on lines and racks.

blocks.text: We shot on location, in a space that came with a fair amount of furniture. I used it to turn the space into a studio apartment: a room without boundaries, with every part of a home crammed into it. We brought in piles of clutter and clothing, and placed the furniture so the room read smaller, as if Emily had built some of the barriers herself to shield part of who she is. I wanted dressing at every level of height: clutter on the floor, along the walls, and hanging down from above the camera, so the room wraps around her and engulfs her.

imgs.alt: On set: the dressed room, from the floor to the lines overhead
On set: the dressed room, from the floor to the lines overhead

blocks.caption: On set: the dressed room, from the floor to the lines overhead.

blocks.text: The bed, usually the most intimate place in a room, sits against the outside wall under her large window. Sex work asks her to expose her rawest self, and she's used to it. It's also from that raw state that she looks out at the world, hoping, expecting. The couch, shielded behind the clothing racks, is the homey corner: the belonging she wants more, deep down.

imgs.alt: Drafted plan and elevations
¾ concept of the room
SketchUp model of the room, built from the drafted plan
A view inside the model from the couch corner toward the doorway

blocks.caption: Top to bottom: drafted plan and elevations; ¾ concept of the room; SketchUp model of the room, built from the drafted plan; a view inside the model from the couch corner toward the doorway.

blocks.caption: Emily asleep on the bed beneath the window.

blocks.text: The characters face an enormous threat from outside, and much of the film watches it from within: from inside the room, looking out. That dynamic, knowing the world from an interior view, was what interested me most.
